e.t: This word means “to praise,” referring to the act of expressing honor or approval. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, appearing in Luke, Acts, Romans, and Revelation. Its use is connected with praise offered in different settings, but the exact object and force of the praise depend on the surrounding verse. The word’s central idea remains straightforward: to praise someone or something openly.

This word means “end,” referring to the concluding point or limit of something. It is used six times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in four verses. Its occurrences are found in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Hebrews, so its basic meaning is consistent across several kinds of New Testament writing. The surrounding verse determines what has reached its end, but the word itself points to an endpoint or final boundary.

This Greek New Testament word means “wind” or “winds,” referring to moving air in the natural world. It is a noun used for the wind as a real, observable force. The word occurs 31 times in the Greek New Testament, showing regular use in descriptions of weather and the natural environment. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is simply wind or winds.

e.t: This word means from above, from the beginning, or again. It is an adverb that can point to a higher origin or starting point, and it can also describe something happening anew. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 13 times across 13 verses, including several uses in John. Its exact sense is determined by the sentence: it may emphasize where something comes from, when it began, or that it happens another time.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means acting “harshly” or “severely.” As an adverb, it describes the manner in which someone speaks or acts, emphasizing firmness that may feel stern or sharp rather than gentle. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Corinthians and Titus. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is clear: something is done in a notably severe or uncompromising way.

This word means a greeting or salutation—the spoken or expressed welcome offered when people meet or address one another. It names the greeting itself rather than the person giving it, and it can describe a formal public greeting as well as an ordinary personal welcome. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, including passages where greetings are sought or offered in public settings and personal encounters.

“Ungrateful” describes someone who does not respond with thankfulness for what has been given or done for them. It identifies a failure of gratitude and is used as a description of people. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs twice, in Luke 6:35 and 2 Timothy 3:2. Its central meaning remains the same in both places: a person marked by lack of thankful response. The surrounding verse determines what particular kindness, gift, or relationship makes the ingratitude visible.

Barsabbas is a personal name, identifying someone rather than describing a quality, action, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in Acts. The available wording gives the name itself, without an additional short definition or meaning phrase. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context, but its basic lexical function is to identify a person named Barsabbas.

This word means a baby or infant—a very young child. It is a noun used for babies from early infancy, including the infant Jesus and children brought to Jesus. It can also describe a newborn or very young child in general, without itself stating anything about the child’s condition or character. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, with most occurrences in Luke. The same word is also used figuratively in 1 Peter for those who are newly beginning in faith, where the surrounding context determines that extended sense.

Gaius is a personal name, referring to a man rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name appears five times in the Greek New Testament, and each occurrence is rendered “Gaius.” It refers to individuals mentioned in Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, and 3 John. Because the name appears in several passages, the surrounding context is needed to distinguish which Gaius is meant in a particular verse.

This Greek New Testament word means “clear,” describing something that is plain and readily recognizable rather than hidden or obscure. It occurs three times in the New Testament, showing a focused meaning rather than a broad range of uses. The word appears in Matthew, 1 Corinthians, and Galatians, but its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording and argument.

This word describes someone or something firm, steadfast, and not easily moved. It points to settled commitment and dependable stability rather than temporary enthusiasm or uncertain effort. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, including passages that speak of remaining firmly committed and standing securely in faithful work. As an adjective, it describes the character or condition of a person or thing. Its exact emphasis in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is clear: remaining firmly established and dependable.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word describes putting something on, throwing something over, seizing, or taking hold of something. Its meaning depends on what action the sentence describes: it can refer to placing clothing or material over something, grasping or taking someone, or an act connected with weeping. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek New Testament, across 18 verses, so its central idea is an active placing, covering, taking, or expressing action rather than a single narrow object or situation. The surrounding verse determines which sense is intended.

This word means “supply” or “support”: providing what is needed so something or someone can be strengthened and carried forward. It presents help as an active provision rather than merely a desire to help. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, showing this is a focused word used in a small number of passages. Its central idea remains the strengthening provision that enables continued growth, service, or endurance.

This word means beauty—the quality of being pleasing in appearance or presentation. It names an attractive outward quality rather than an action or command. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 1:11, and its English rendering there is “beauty.” The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the pleasant, attractive quality indicated by the gloss.

“Mortal” describes a person or body that is subject to death and does not possess everlasting life by nature. It identifies the temporary, death-bound condition of human existence. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs six times, describing what belongs to mortal human life or the mortal body. Its basic meaning remains consistent across its uses, while the surrounding passage explains the particular point being made about mortality, weakness, or the hope of change.

This word means “Jerusalem,” the name of the city central to many New Testament events and references. It functions as a proper name rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 77 times, appearing especially often in Acts and Luke. The word may refer to the city itself in different passages, while the precise significance of each mention depends on its surrounding verse and context.

Cainan is a personal name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke 3:36–37, within the genealogy recorded there. The name is rendered consistently as “Cainan.” Its precise significance in the genealogy comes from the surrounding names and passage, but the word itself functions simply as this person’s name.

This word means “Cyprus,” the name of a place mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a geographical name rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It occurs five times, all in Acts, including references to travel and movement involving Cyprus. The word therefore identifies the place itself; the specific significance of Cyprus in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and account.

This word means “pearl” or “pearls,” referring to a valuable gem formed in the sea and prized for its beauty. It is a noun used for pearls as individual objects or as a collection. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, including passages that mention pearls among valuable possessions, costly adornment, and precious merchandise. Its meaning remains straightforward across these uses: a pearl is an expensive, beautiful object whose worth makes it suitable for comparison with something greatly valued.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to testify” or “it is testified,” referring to giving witness or affirming something before others. It is used for bearing witness concerning a person, facts, or a truth, with the exact force shaped by the surrounding verse. The word occurs 76 times in the Greek New Testament, across 72 verses. “Testify” is its main English rendering and closely expresses its central meaning.

e.t: This word means “to deport” or “to send to another place.” It describes moving people away from their present location, especially by directing or forcing them to settle elsewhere. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts 7. Its basic sense is the removal of people from one place to another; the surrounding verse determines the specific historical situation and force of the action.

This Greek New Testament word means “abode” or “room,” referring to a place where someone lives or stays. It describes a dwelling place, not an action, person, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, and both occurrences are in John 14. Its basic sense remains focused on a place of residence; the surrounding verse determines the particular significance intended in each occurrence.

This word refers to a person affected by paralysis—a paralytic. It is used as a noun describing someone whose movement is impaired by this condition, rather than naming the condition itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, all in Matthew and Mark. The word appears in accounts involving people brought to Jesus or described among those needing healing, though its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its central meaning remains straightforward: a person unable to move normally because of paralysis.

This word refers to “fullness” or “fulfillment”—the condition of something being filled or brought to its intended fullness. It can describe fullness as a state or fulfillment as an achieved result, depending on how it functions in a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 17 times, so its central idea appears across several kinds of statements rather than belonging to only one narrow setting. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on fullness itself or on fulfillment being reached.

e.t: This word means “to predict,” describing the act of declaring something before it happens. It functions as an action word focused on what is to come, rather than on noticing or reporting something afterward. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Peter 1:11. The precise force in that sentence depends on its surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the advance announcement or prediction of an event.

This Greek New Testament word means “fist,” referring to a hand closed tightly. It is a specific word for the hand in that clenched condition, rather than a general term for the hand itself. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 7:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning remains “fist.”

This word means a gate or gates, referring to an entrance or movable barrier that gives access to a place. It can describe one gate or more than one, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek New Testament, including references to entrances associated with homes, cities, or other locations. Its basic meaning remains concrete and straightforward: a gate is the point of entry or passage into an enclosed or defined place.

This word means a scorpion, the stinging creature known for its poisonous sting. It is a noun referring to one such creature or to scorpions collectively. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times: twice in Luke and three times in Revelation. The word’s basic meaning remains the same in each occurrence, while the surrounding passage determines whether the reference is to ordinary creatures or to figures used in a vision. Scripture’s use of the word therefore presents the scorpion as a recognizable image of danger and painful harm.

This word means a fellow countryman or one’s own countrymen—people who belong to the same country or homeland. It is a noun referring to someone connected by national origin, rather than simply any companion or neighbor. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Thessalonians 2:14. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is a person’s own countrymen.

e.t: This word means “be next to” or “to be next door to.” It describes being situated immediately beside another person, place, or thing. As a verb, it expresses close physical nearness rather than a distant or general association. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 18:7. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic sense is clear: something or someone is located right beside another.

This Greek New Testament word means “saving,” referring to rescue or deliverance. It describes salvation as something that brings a person safely out of danger or loss and into a saved condition. The word appears five times in the Greek New Testament, including passages that speak of seeing God’s salvation, salvation reaching the nations, salvation as a helmet, and grace appearing to bring salvation. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains saving deliverance.

e.t: This word means “perhaps,” expressing possibility rather than certainty. It introduces something that may happen or may be true, while leaving the outcome open. In ordinary English, it can be understood as “possibly” or “maybe,” but “perhaps” is the directly attested meaning here. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Romans and Philemon. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic function remains to present a possibility without asserting it as definite.

e.t: This word means to feed, provide nourishment, or care for someone or something. It can describe supplying what is needed for life and growth, whether the object is a person, an animal, or another living thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, including passages about birds being fed and people caring for others. Its sense may therefore include both the practical act of feeding and the broader responsibility of tending or providing care.

This word means “ghost,” referring to an apparition or spirit-like figure perceived by people. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, once in Matthew and once in Mark. Both occurrences use the same basic meaning, describing what the disciples thought they saw when they noticed Jesus. The word identifies the perceived figure; the surrounding passage is needed to explain the full event in each verse.

This word means “natural” or “physical,” describing what belongs to ordinary created life rather than something beyond the natural sphere. It functions as an adjective, identifying a person, body, or source according to its natural or physical character. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, especially in 1 Corinthians, and is also found in James and Jude. Its exact force in any verse depends on the noun or idea it describes.
